how-much-to-charge-for-a-paver-patio.htm.text:
← Paver patio bid calculator

How much to charge for a paver patio

The number a homeowner wants is a price per square foot of patio. That number is not a takeoff. A 12 × 16 running-bond sitting area on six inches of compacted base is not the same job as 12 × 16 of 45° herringbone on a ten-inch driveway pad. The face is identical. The hole, the waste, the cuts, and the dump tickets are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Price the hole, then the face

Excavation depth is base + bedding + paver thickness. On the sample rates shipped with the calculator, a 12 × 16 patio at 6 inches of base excavates about 5.6 cubic yards. The same face at 10 inches of base excavates about 7.9. If spoils cannot stay on site, that extra yardage is also a dump ticket. Quoting both jobs at the same per-foot number is how the driveway pad eats the patio margin.

Pattern waste is material; extra cuts are labor

Running bond often starts around 7% extra pavers. 90° herringbone around 10%. 45° herringbone around 15%. Circular or fan layouts around 18%. Those extra pavers do not, by themselves, add hours — the crew still walks the finished face. The extra hours come from the cut list, which is why the calculator keeps a separate pattern labor factor. Mixing the two hides which part of a high bid is stone and which part is time.

Edge restraint does not care how big the patio is

A 12 × 16 rectangle has 56 feet of edge. A 4 × 40 walkway has 88 feet of edge on the same 160 square feet. Soldier courses, interior radii, and seat-wall returns add lineal feet that a per-square-foot special never sees. Measure the restraint, or you are giving away the plastic, the spikes, and the hours that hold the field together.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $32/h crew loaded at 30% payroll burden is $41.60. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample 12 × 16 running-bond patio the calculator prices about $4,381 ($22.82 per finished square foot, 20.9 crew-hours, walk-away $3,417). The same face as 45° herringbone on a 10-inch base prices about $5,151 ($26.83 per foot). Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not an engineered pavement design, a soils report, a permit, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Compaction spec, drainage, polymeric-sand joint width, and local code are yours to confirm.

Price your patio

Common questions

How much to charge for a paver patio?

Charge from finished area plus pattern waste, compacted-base cubic yards, edge restraint, haul-away, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 12 × 16 running-bond patio on a 6-inch base prices around $22–$23 per finished square foot on the sample rates in this calculator — the same face as 45° herringbone on a 10-inch driveway pad is several dollars more per foot.

Why is a per-square-foot paver quote dangerous?

Homeowners measure the face they walk on. Pattern waste, excavation volume, dump tickets, and edge restraint do not scale with that face. Matching a cheaper per-foot quote written for a simple running-bond patio is how a herringbone driveway pad becomes a loss.

How much extra paver should I buy for herringbone?

Start around 7% for running bond, 10% for 90° herringbone, 15% for 45° herringbone, and 18% for circular or fan layouts. Those are starting points, not a manufacturer warranty — a border course and a lot of radii move the number.

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not engineering, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

FOR HARDSCAPE / PAVER CONTRACTORS

Bid the base and the waste, not the square footage.

A flat per-square-foot quote treats a 12 × 16 running-bond patio as the same job as 12 × 16 of 45° herringbone on a 10-inch driveway pad. Pattern waste, excavation volume, haul-away, and edge restraint do not scale with the face the homeowner measures. Price those extras separately, then see the walk-away number.

The patio

Start from a common job, then replace every rate with numbers from your own crew and invoices. Picking a pattern fills waste and extra-cut labor only if you have not already changed them.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, liability insurance, and paid time off. A $32/h crew loaded at 30% is $41.60. Quoting the raw wage is how a per-foot special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first dump ticket.

Hand the customer a proposal

The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the homeowner — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

Where the cost goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. Pattern waste and base depths are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a pavement design — replace them with your own takeoff.

    Common questions

    Why can't I just quote a paver patio per square foot?

    Because the square footage the homeowner measures is the finished face, and three of the biggest costs do not follow it. Pattern waste and cut labor follow the layout. Excavation and haul-away follow the volume under the patio, which is area × base depth. Edge restraint follows the perimeter. A 12 × 16 running-bond patio and 192 sq ft of 45° herringbone on a driveway section have the same face and are not the same job.

    How much does the laying pattern actually change the price?

    Two ways at once, which is why patterns are worth pricing rather than eyeballing. Waste: running bond starts at 7%, 90° herringbone 10%, 45° herringbone 15%, circular or random 18%. Labor: the same patterns carry factors of 1.0, 1.15, 1.25, and 1.35 on install hours. So moving from running bond to a 45° herringbone buys about 8 points more material and a quarter more labor — and both come out of the same per-foot number a competitor quoted.

    Why is a driveway priced differently from a patio of the same size?

    Base depth. A patio or walkway starts at 6 in of base; a driveway or parking pad at 10 in. That is not a small adjustment: excavation volume, stone tonnage, and haul-away all scale with depth, so the same face area digs out and hauls off roughly two-thirds more material. These are common starting depths you can change, not a pavement design — soil, frost depth, and load are your call and your jurisdiction's, not this page's.

    Does haul-away make much difference?

    Enough to decide a bid. Excavated volume comes out as cubic yards from area and base depth, and hauling it costs both trucking and dump fees on top of the excavation hours themselves. Turning haul-away off — spreading spoil on site, when the site allows it — is one of the few levers that moves a paver bid materially without changing what the customer receives. The tool shows the gap rather than assuming either way.

    Why is edge restraint priced separately from the pavers?

    Because it is bought by the linear foot of perimeter, and perimeter does not track area. A long narrow walkway has far more edge per square foot than a square patio of the same size — a 4 × 40 walkway is 160 sq ft with 88 ft of edge, while a 12 × 16 patio is 192 sq ft with 56. Polymeric sand is counted the same careful way: whole bags, rounded up from your own coverage figure.

    Why isn't a 25% margin the same as adding 25% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — which is how the quote reads to the homeowner and how your books read it. Overhead is a separate markup on direct cost, applied before margin and never to itself or to profit. A $6,000 cost marked up 25% is $7,500, a 20% margin; a 25% target margin is $8,000. Nothing leaves your browser — no account, no upload, and the optional local counter records only which features were used and the day.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-square-foot.html.text:
← Paver Patio Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per square foot

“$X a square foot, any hardscape job” is not a price for a patio build — it is a price for one base depth, one pattern, and one haul-away situation, quietly applied to a driveway pad two and a half times the area that needs a deeper base, a fussier pattern, and a dump run the coupon never saw.

What a flat rate per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a hardscape job over the phone: multiply the finished face by a number and read it back. Homeowners like it because it is easy to compare against a competitor's quote, and it is the number a customer holding one will ask you to match.

The number behind it was usually set for the simplest version of the job — a small patio at the minimum base depth, a plain running-bond pattern, and spoils left on site — and then reused for every job afterward, whether or not the next one is a driveway pad on a deeper base, a pattern that wastes more material and takes longer to cut, or a lot too tight to leave the dug-out base material behind.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the length and width (or area), the pattern, the base depth, edge restraint, and whether spoils need to be hauled away, plus your own wage, payroll burden, material costs, overhead, and target margin. It prices pavers by the square foot including pattern waste, base and bedding by the cubic yard from the actual excavation depth, edge restraint by the lineal foot, and haul-away from the actual excavation volume — for this job, not a flat rate for every job.

What a flat rate per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same per square foot whether the job sits on 6 inches of base for foot traffic or 10 inches for a driveway pad. Prices base and bedding by the cubic yard from the actual excavation depth the selected use requires, not a single depth for every job.
Has no line for pattern waste or the extra cutting time a fussier layout adds, even though a circular or herringbone pattern buys and cuts more pavers per finished square foot than running bond. Prices pavers on the finished area plus pattern waste, and applies a separate labor factor for the extra cuts each pattern needs.
Has no line for edge restraint, even though lineal feet of perimeter does not scale with area the way a long, narrow walkway shows. Prices edge restraint from the actual perimeter (or an entered edge length) as its own line, separate from the paved face.
Has no line for hauling spoils off site, even though a tight lot with nowhere to dump the dug-out base material adds a real trucking cost a backyard patio never needed. Prices haul-away from the actual excavation volume as its own line, only when the job needs it.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price, the profit, and the effective hourly rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two jobs, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own figures, at a 22% target margin, a $32 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, and $375 in travel and equipment:

A 12 × 16 ft running-bond patio on 6 inches of base with spoils left on site costs $3,065.87 to run and this calculator prices it at $3,930.60 — $20.47 per square foot. A 20 × 24 ft circular driveway pad on 10 inches of base — more pattern waste, a slower cutting pace, and a haul-away run — costs $9,259.22 to run and this calculator prices it at $11,870.79, 3.02 times the patio's price on just 2.5 times the area. Quote the driveway pad at the patio's flat $20.47-per-square-foot rate instead, and 480 square feet prices at $9,826.50 — still above the job's $9,259.22 break-even cost, but by only $567.28, and $2,044.29 short of what this calculator prices the job at. A contractor targeting a 22% margin on that rate actually realizes about 5.8%, most of it eaten by the deeper base, the extra waste, and the haul-away the flat rate never priced.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per square foot get a bigger or different job wrong?

Because finished square footage is the face the homeowner measures, not the hole under it or the parts list. A flat rate is usually set on a small patio at the minimum base depth with a simple pattern and spoils left on site; a driveway pad needs a deeper base, a fussier pattern wastes more pavers and costs more labor per square foot, and hauling spoils off site is its own line the coupon never counted. Using this calculator's own figures, a 12 x 16 running-bond patio on 6 inches of base with spoils left on site costs $3,065.87 to run and this calculator prices it at $3,930.60 -- $20.47 per square foot. A 20 x 24 circular driveway pad on 10 inches of base with haul-away costs $9,259.22 to run and this calculator prices it at $11,870.79 -- 3.02 times the patio's price, not 2.5 times, on 2.5 times the finished area.

What does a flat rate per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Base depth, pattern waste, edge restraint, and haul-away. A flat per-square-foot rate has no line for the extra excavation and compacted base a driveway pad needs over a patio, no line for the higher paver waste and slower cutting a circular or herringbone pattern adds over running bond, no line for edge restraint scaling with perimeter rather than area, and no line for trucking spoils off site when they cannot stay in the yard.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own figures: the 12 x 16 running-bond patio prices at $3,930.60, on a job that costs $3,065.87 to run, at $20.47 per square foot. Apply that same per-square-foot rate to the 480-square-foot circular driveway pad and it quotes at $9,826.50 -- $2,044.29 short of what this calculator prices the job at ($11,870.79). The job still clears its $9,259.22 break-even cost, but only by $567.28: a contractor pricing off the patio's rate and targeting a 22% margin actually realizes about 5.8%, most of it consumed by the deeper base, the extra waste, and the haul-away the flat rate never priced.

Is a flat rate per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a job close to the base depth, pattern, and haul-away situation the rate was set on -- typically a simple patio at minimum base depth in running bond with spoils left on site -- a flat per-square-foot number can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a driveway pad, a fussier pattern, or a job that needs haul-away at the same rate, because the rate does not know the base depth, the pattern, or where the spoils go until someone measures the site, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted over the phone.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's material pricing, or what other hardscape contractors in your area charge. It takes length and width (or area), pattern, base depth, edge restraint, haul-away, and your own wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat rate per square foot skips, not a market survey.

vs-aspire.html.text:
← Paver Patio Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Aspire

Two different shapes: Aspire is an account-based business-management platform for running a hardscape or landscape company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this paver patio cost, given its face, pattern, base, and edge — before you send the bid.

What each tool is for

Aspire is a cloud business-management platform, founded in 2013 by Kevin Kehoe and Mark Tipton, headquartered in Chesterfield, Missouri. It is built for landscape maintenance and construction contractors — including hardscape and paver installation crews — as well as irrigation, snow and ice management, and commercial cleaning companies, and has been part of ServiceTitan since ServiceTitan's 2021 acquisition of it. It bundles CRM and lead tracking, estimating, scheduling, purchasing, job costing, mobile crew time tracking, invoicing, and accounting and payroll integration into one ongoing subscription account, with a mobile app for crews in the field. Its own plans are tiered by a contractor's annual revenue rather than sold at one flat price, and no dollar figure for any plan is published on its site — pricing is reached by requesting a demo. Aspire's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact tier names or any dollar figure, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a business-management platform serving landscape construction, irrigation, snow and ice, and cleaning contractors, sold as a revenue-tiered subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Aspire appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Aspire does. It does not track a lead, schedule a crew, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one patio — length and width, laying pattern (running bond through 45° herringbone), base depth, bedding sand, edge restraint footage, and whether excavated spoils are hauled off site — plus loaded crew cost, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the install price, the price per finished square foot, the effective crew hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one patio. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Most hardscape and landscape companies get different value from each: Aspire (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole lead-to-invoice operation as an ongoing, revenue-tiered subscription, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login answer to what one paver patio should cost from its face, pattern, and base before a business system is involved. Should I use this calculator or Aspire?

They do different jobs, and a hardscape or landscape company of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
